data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)\right]+10 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 14\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 14\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-5)\right]+10=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+10

=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+10=12

So the model gives exactly \boxed{12.0\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (9:00 a.m.):

d(9)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+9=6\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+9

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 5:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=15+6=21\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=15-6=9\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 21\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 9\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[9\text{ ft},\ 21\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (5:00 a.m.):

d(5)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+15=6\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+15

=6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+15=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2}+15

So the model gives approximately \boxed{20.2\text{ ft}} at 5:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=11, so the water averages \boxed{11\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=11+4=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-4=7\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

d(9)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+11=4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+11

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+4=13\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-4=5\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 13\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 13\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+9=4\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+9

=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+9=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+9

So the model gives approximately \boxed{5.5\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=11, so the water averages \boxed{11\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=11+4=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-4=7\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-5)\right]+11=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+11

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=11, so the water averages \boxed{11\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=11+6=17\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-6=5\text{ ft}

High tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-4)\right]+11=6\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+11

=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+11=-\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2}+11

So the model gives approximately \boxed{5.8\text{ ft}} at noon.

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+6=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-6=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 8:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+6=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-6=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=8 (8:00 a.m.):

d(8)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(8-3)\right]+12=6\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+12

=6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=15

So the model gives exactly \boxed{15.0\text{ ft}} at 8:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+6=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-6=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

\text{maximum}=11+6=17\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-6=5\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 17\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 17\text{ ft}]}.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=13, so the water averages \boxed{13\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=13+6=19\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=13-6=7\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=11, so the water averages \boxed{11\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=11+4=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-4=7\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 7\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[7\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-2)\right]+11=4\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+11

=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+11=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+11

So the model gives approximately \boxed{7.5\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 14\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 14\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 11:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (11:00 a.m.):

d(11)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+10=6\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+10

=6\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+10=-\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2}+10

So the model gives approximately \boxed{4.8\text{ ft}} at 11:00 a.m..

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=15+4=19\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=15-4=11\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 11\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[11\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+4=14\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-4=6\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 14\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 6\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 14\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 5:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=15, so the water averages \boxed{15\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=15+4=19\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=15-4=11\text{ ft}

High tide is at 7:00 a.m., when the depth is 19\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 1:00 p.m., when the depth is 11\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[11\text{ ft},\ 19\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

The phase shift is \boxed{4} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 4 hours to the right: at 4:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 7:00 a.m. and again at 7:00 p.m.; low tide is at 1:00 p.m. and again at 1:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (5:00 a.m.):

d(5)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-4)\right]+15=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+15

=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+15=17

So the model gives exactly \boxed{17.0\text{ ft}} at 5:00 a.m..

\text{maximum}=11+4=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=11-4=7\text{ ft}

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 5:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+6=20\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-6=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 20\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 20\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=5 (5:00 a.m.):

d(5)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(5-3)\right]+14=6\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+14

=6\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=\frac{6\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

So the model gives approximately \boxed{19.2\text{ ft}} at 5:00 a.m..

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

d(9)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+10=6\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+10

data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at noon. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-5)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+12

=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=10

So the model gives exactly \boxed{10.0\text{ ft}} at noon.

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-5)\right]+15=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+15

=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+15=17

So the model gives exactly \boxed{17.0\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)\right]+9 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.
data.part_a: What is the average depth of the water at this harbor?
data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 9:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+4=13\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-4=5\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 13\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 13\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (9:00 a.m.):

d(9)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-5)\right]+9=4\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+9

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+9=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+9

So the model gives approximately \boxed{12.5\text{ ft}} at 9:00 a.m..
